THE AXIS DOES NOT EXIST AT ALL FOR A US APPLIANCE PANEL (explained by Andriy 2026-08-21): Europe builds the fridge INSIDE a cabinet, so the cabinet holds the hinges and its door is linked to the appliance door by a bracket - the hand belongs to the cabinet and the factory must be told it. America stands the fridge in a housing between neighbouring cabinets or panels and mounts the panel straight onto the appliance, so the hand is decided by the machine and the factory has no part in it. hinge_side must never be ORDERED for an appliance_front that mounts on the machine - printed p.418 says '1 door' because the article has no hand to state, not because the page is incomplete. THE DRAWING IS A SEPARATE MATTER and carries the hand anyway: fridges hinge one way and freezers the other, clients sometimes swap them, and since the estimate cannot record a hand the elevation is the only place the installer can read it. So the axis is absent from the ORDER and present on the DRAWING - see families.'USA Tall H.210'. The dishwasher door on printed p.47 is the same relationship read from the other end: it bolts to the machine's own door, so its axis is a constant of the appliance class. requires.scope: COMPOSITION, NOT UNIT - and this is why no filter was built. The grip system is chosen once for the whole kitchen: estimate 2026/30829 sets it in the header ('L-Shaped' grip horizontal in Matt Aluminium). So whether Lume may be offered is a property of the PROJECT, not of the selected cabinet, and a per-unit filter would be a rule generalising past its evidence. Even the tempting case - a family that declares no gola version at all, like Tall H.210 - is not decided by the page, which never says a handle unit cannot sit in a straight-grip composition. This waits on M1.6 project defaults, which is where the composition axes live. Recorded as DATA so the filter has something to read the day M1.6 lands; until then the picker offers Lume like every other handle, and that gap is deliberate and pinned by a test.

hardware.um_note: UNIT OF MEASURE, added 2026-08-22 for the exporter. The factory estimate uses three: PZ (piece), ML (linear metre), MQ (square metre), and a quantity of 1 means one piece, one metre's worth or one square metre's worth depending on the row - so an exporter that assumes 1 = one thing is wrong on a large part of the sheet. THE TWO ENTRIES HERE DO NOT HAVE THE SAME AUTHORITY. ML on the gola profiles is CONFIRMED: estimate 2026/30829 prices GOL001 and GOL002 per linear metre, and factory output outranks the price list. PZ on the handles is OUR READING at CONTROL: the estimate's UM table names PZ for units, fronts, tops and plinth and does not mention handles at all; a handle is plainly a piece, but nobody has shown us the row. The estimate now going to Elda will show both directly. QUANTITY IS A SEPARATE QUESTION and is deliberately not answered here: an ML line is quantified by the RUN, not by the cabinet, and a PZ handle line by how many fronts the unit has - neither is a property of the article, so the exporter emits those quantities as nil rather than inventing a 1.
hardware.gola_note: position=undercounter profiles (GOL001 L-shaped / GOL005 straight) are the valid choice for a base-unit front under the worktop; intermediate profiles join stacked front zones and are NOT offered for single-door base units. Source: 'Do not add 57 to carcass height' - the profile lives in the 30 mm gola zone, the carcass does not grow. Cross-restriction: handle Lume M00014 - held as DATA in hardware.handles M00014.requires, with its page and its scope. It is deliberately not restated here: a restriction written in two places is a restriction that goes stale in one of them.

wine_cooler_panel_apertures.provenance: Three manufacturer specification sheets supplied by Andriy 2026-08-22. NOT Cesar facts - kept outside the four-level trust model, exactly like the LEGRABOX table. Cesar dimensions the aperture nowhere; these are what the appliance makers publish.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.why_it_is_here: A panel-ready wine cooler needs a hole in its front, and the hole belongs to the MACHINE, not to the article. This table is the seed of the appliance module: when appliances are modelled, a wine cooler brings its three rails with it and the front stops guessing. Until then registry/cesar/usa_tall_h210.json takes a default from here and marks it indicative.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.form: Every maker dimensions the RAILS - the frame left of, right of, above and below the hole - and lets the aperture follow. Rails are what stay constant when the panel width changes, which is why the aperture is derived and never stored.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.columns: panel_w_mm / panel_h_mm / rail_side_mm / rail_top_mm / rail_bottom_mm / aperture_mm (derived)

rows.source: Miele USA spec sheet 2020-02-13, 'Custom Panel for Inset Design'
rows.note: Aperture width printed as '383 max' - a ceiling, not a point. A 60 cm European column; its panel is 1762 tall and never carries a 2100 front.
Lateral rail explicitly a RANGE: 74 to 82 mm. Panel thickness 19.
Identical rails to the 18 inch unit - only the panel width changes. So the rails are a property of the PRODUCT LINE, not of the width.

wine_cooler_panel_apertures.what_converges: rail_side 79 / 79 / 84 and rail_top 155 / 158 / 158, across two unrelated makers, as absolute millimetres and not as proportions of the panel (84/551 = 15.2 %, 79/451 = 17.5 %, 79/603 = 13.1 %). Two numbers that agree to within 5 mm.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.what_does_not: rail_bottom: 111 against 243, a factor of 2.2. That is where the machine compartment and the presenter drawer sit, and it is genuinely per-appliance. It is the one number that must come from the machine.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.consequence_for_the_datum: The aperture is dimensioned from the bottom edge by habit, but the bottom rail is the unstable one - so anchoring at the bottom moves the whole hole when the guess is wrong, while anchoring at the top and the sides leaves only the aperture's lower edge undetermined. Recorded because it inverts the obvious choice.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.tolerance: Both makers state the aperture as a window, not a point: Thermador allows the lateral rail anywhere between 74 and 82 mm, Miele prints its aperture width as '383 max'. Being a few millimetres out is inside the makers' own latitude - which is why an indicative rectangle is worth drawing at all.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.what_is_still_open: Panel heights are 1762 and 2029; a Cesar CR94xx front is 2100. So where the appliance's own panel rectangle sits inside our front is not settled. Parked with the appliance model, beside the fridge door swing projection.
wine_cooler_panel_apertures.width_cross_check: Thermador's 24 inch panel is 603 wide and Cesar's CR9601 is 610; the 18 inch pair is 451 against 457. The 6-7 mm is the reveal we decided not to draw, so the Cesar width is the NICHE and our decision to draw the nominal is confirmed from the appliance side.

panel_thickness_conflict.raised_by: Andriy, 2026-08-22, on the drawing: a thicker door swings wider, and the leaf can foul its neighbour.
panel_thickness_conflict.cesar: 2.2 cm. Standards::FRONT_T_MM = 22, elda_confirmed. Not changed by any of this.
panel_thickness_conflict.thermador: 'The drawing is based on a door panel thickness of 3/4" (19 mm)', and the maximum panel dimensions are computed from a 1/8" (3 mm) clearance. 19 is stated flat, with no alternative offered.
panel_thickness_conflict.miele: 16 to 22 mm are all permitted, and the maker answers the swing question directly: a table of MINIMUM GAP X to the ADJOINING HOUSING UNIT DOOR, by panel thickness and by the panel's edge radius B.
panel_thickness_conflict.what_it_means: A 22 mm Cesar front is not forbidden - Miele explicitly allows it - but it costs gap: 6.5 mm beside it instead of 3, unless the front carries an edge radius. Thermador does not offer the choice at all, which is the real risk: its clearances are planned around 19. So this is a QUESTION FOR THE FACTORY, not a number to change here.
panel_thickness_conflict.elda_question: Can the USA appliance panels (CR94xx / CR96xx and their siblings) be supplied at 19 mm instead of 22, or is 2.2 cm the only thickness? If 22 is fixed, what edge radius do they carry, so the required gap can be read off the appliance maker's table?
panel_thickness_conflict.not_done: Standards::FRONT_T_MM stays 22 and the open leaf is still drawn at 22. 70_symbols already carries the note that a 19 mm US front would be one change in one place - it is not made on a suspicion.

wall_hung.construction_note: A wall-hung base unit is NOT 'without feet'. CESAR - 1 Project Guidelines.pdf printed p.39: 'Wall-hung base units are always provided with fixings and a foot to stabilise them and determine their inclination.' The rendered drawing (sources/factory/pg-p39-wallhung.png) shows the fixing at the top rear and the foot at the BOTTOM REAR bearing against the WALL, where it sets the tilt; it never touches the floor. So: no floor contact and no plinth, but a foot exists and it occupies clearance behind the carcass.
